name: Preference Tuning with DPO
question: How do I teach a model which answer is better?
summary: Direct Preference Optimization trains on pairs: for each prompt, a chosen and a rejected answer. It raises the likelihood of chosen answers relative to rejected ones while a parameter, beta, keeps the model close to a reference, without training a separate reward model as RLHF does. It usually follows SFT, and it learns whatever the pairs share, including biases such as longer answers always being chosen.
useCases: Behaviour that is easier to compare than to write, such as helpfulness or tone
Fixing a known failure with pairs of good and bad responses
Aligning with reviewers’ or customers’ preferences

items.detail: prompt, chosen, rejected; from human raters or a calibrated AI judge
lower moves further from the reference; TRL’s default is 0.1
no reward model or PPO loop; simpler and more stable
usually after SFT, which teaches the basic format
disagreeing annotators weaken or reverse the signal
if chosen answers are longer, the model learns to ramble

steps: Start from an SFT model that already follows the format
Collect pairs with clear, consistent preference criteria
Check pairs for bias, such as length, and for annotator agreement
Train with a moderate beta and compare win rate and regressions
pitfalls: Noisy or inconsistent preferences, so the signal cancels out
Chosen answers systematically longer, teaching verbosity
Beta so low that the model drifts and loses general skills
remember: Clean pairs, moderate beta, watch length and regressions.

steps.title: Collect preference pairs
steps.text: For each question, advisers saw two answers and chose the better one. Judging is quicker and more consistent than writing ideal answers.

steps.title: Drop pairs people disagree on
steps.text: Pairs where reviewers disagreed are close to coin flips. Every mislabelled pair cancels a correct one, so cleaning beats collecting more.

steps.title: Start from an SFT model
steps.text: DPO refines a model that already follows instructions. On a raw base model it has too much to learn from preferences alone.

steps.title: Set beta
steps.text: beta keeps the model near the frozen reference. Too small, and it drifts and loses general skills; too large, and it barely changes. 0.1 is a common start.

steps.title: Balance answer lengths
steps.text: If the chosen answer is usually the longer one, the model learns that length wins. The first run here did exactly that.

steps.title: Report more than the win rate
steps.text: Win rate against the old model rose from 50% to 64%. Answer length and a general regression suite show whether that came at a cost.

practice.scenario: A wealth-tech firm’s research assistant gave correct but rambling answers that advisers rated below a competitor’s. Advisers compared pairs of answers for 5,000 questions. DPO on top of the existing SFT model raised the win rate against the old model from 50% to 64%. The first run had preferred longer answers every time; after balancing lengths in the pairs, gains held and answers were 8% shorter.

industries.use: Answers advisers prefer: concise, hedged, with the key number first
Replies that resolve rather than deflect, judged by agents

practice.analogy: Teaching by comparison: instead of writing a perfect answer, a senior colleague looks at two drafts and says which is better. Many such judgements shape taste faster than one model answer.

library.name: Hugging Face TRL
library.what: DPOTrainer takes a dataset with prompt, chosen and rejected columns and optimises the model directly on the preferences, with no separate reward model.

practice.note: beta controls how far the model may move from the reference. Check the length of answers and a general regression suite after training, not just the win rate.

samples.code:
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer

pairs = load_dataset("json", data_files="adviser_pairs.jsonl")["train"]
# each row: {"prompt": ..., "chosen": ..., "rejected": ...}
pairs = pairs.filter(lambda r: r["agreement"] >= 0.75)   # drop noisy pairs

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("sft-research-8b")  # start from SFT

trainer = DPOTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=DPOConfig(output_dir="dpo-research", beta=0.1, learning_rate=1e-6,
                   num_train_epochs=1),
    train_dataset=pairs,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear",
                           task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
trainer.train()

numericDrill.question: You have 5,000 preference pairs, and 30% of them are labelled the wrong way round. If each wrong pair cancels one correct pair, how many pairs of net useful signal remain?
numericDrill.answer: Correct pairs: 3,500; wrong: 1,500. Net 3,500 − 1,500 = 2,000, which is 5,000 × (1 − 2 × 0.3). Cleaning labels to 5% noise would give 4,500: more than double the signal from the same collection effort.

interview.question: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
interview.answer: RLHF trains a separate reward model on preferences and then optimises the policy against it with reinforcement learning. DPO skips both: it uses a closed-form loss on chosen and rejected pairs that raises the likelihood of the chosen answer relative to a frozen reference model. It is simpler, more stable and cheaper, though online methods can still do better on some tasks.

interview.question: What does beta control in DPO?
interview.answer: How far the tuned model may drift from the reference. A small beta lets it move a lot, which can win preferences but hurt other skills; a large beta keeps it close, so it learns less. Values around 0.1 are a common starting point.
